title: Studio Ghibli’s No Face twirls to sound of Spirited Away’s theme song in beautiful accessory box
description: This box comes pre-loaded with something for anime fans to treasure. Usually, if you’re buying a box, it’s because you’ve got stuff you want to keep in it, right? And while the box we’re looking at today can, of course, fill that purpose, it’s a pretty safe bet that most people are going to be […]
content:
This box comes pre-loaded with something for anime fans to treasure.

Usually, if you’re buying a box, it’s because you’ve got stuff you want to keep in it, right? And while the box we’re looking at today can, of course, fill that purpose, it’s a pretty safe bet that most people are going to be buying it because of what it already has inside.

The exterior is adorned with illustrations of characters from Studio Ghibli’s beloved anime film Spirited Away. Yubaba is here and so is her underling Yu-Bird, both in its original human-headed avian form and its post-transformation Haedori insect state, the latter carrying the transformed Boh. A trio of Susuwatari Soot Sprites can be spotted hanging out together too.

But stealing the scene, as always, is No Face, standing stoically underneath the flying Haku on the box’s lid…

…and who’s also standing inside the box!

You’ll notice we only said No Face is standing stoically on the outside, though, because the one inside the box can twirl around.

On the back of the box is a wind-up screw, and if you give it a few twists before opening the box’s lid, No Face will gently spin as a music box-rendition of Spirited Away’s ending theme, “Itsumo Nandodemo,” plays.

This being an offering from Studio Ghibli specialty shop Donguri Kyowakoku, going in for a closer look reveals some lovingly detailed craftsmanship.

With total dimensions of 8.5 x 10.5 x 12 centimeters (3.3 x 4.1 x 4.7 inches), the box isn’t going to hold any large-scale treasures, but it’s nicely sized for accessories, house keys, or other personal items, and the two sections help keep things nicely organized.

▼ We’re going to assume that the No Face inside the box is from the later part of the Spirited Away story, where he’s become less covetous and more considerate, the kind of guy who’s less likely to eat your valuables and more likely to pour you some soy sauce.

The Spirited Away Paper Box Music Box, as it’s officially called, is priced at 7,150 yen and is recently returned to availability after a restock, and can be ordered through Donguri Kyowakoku’s online store here.

title: Japanese vending machine sells freshly squeezed lemon juice with a futuristic light show
description: We test the sourness of the juice but get distracted by a surprise performance. Five years ago, Japan’s vending machine scene was taken up a notch with the birth of “Feed Me Orange”, a fresh juice machine that squeezes oranges on the spot. It didn’t take long for the machine to grow from being a […]
content:
We test the sourness of the juice but get distracted by a surprise performance.

Five years ago, Japan’s vending machine scene was taken up a notch with the birth of “Feed Me Orange”, a fresh juice machine that squeezes oranges on the spot. It didn’t take long for the machine to grow from being a rare novelty to a familiar mainstay in shopping centres, proving that Japan really does have a thirst for freshly squeezed citrus from a machine.

▼ Now, though, there’s a new contender on the market, and this time it’s serving up freshly squeezed lemon juice.

Called “Kawagoto Lemon Kouka” (“Peel-and-all Lemon Effect”), our reporter Haruka Takagi stumbled upon the vending machine in Osaka’s Namba area, in among the flashy signs and neon lights of the busy Ebisu Bashi-suji shopping street. She was surprised to see it, because unlike oranges, which have a sweetness to suit a wide range of palates, lemons tend to exist on the more piquant end of the citrus spectrum, making her wonder if a machine like this might serve drinks that are too sour for anyone’s liking.

Taking a closer look, she found that customers can choose from a variety of juice options, all made with lemons from a particular region selected for having the tastiest fruit at that particular time of year. When Haruka visited, the machine was using California-grown lemons, which are said to have a medium level of sweetness and sourness.

▼ Although the lemons were from California when Haruka visited, she’s since heard that Japanese-grown lemons will be used from September onwards.

Looking closely, she read that the sugar used for sweetening the drinks is made from 100-percent natural sugar cane, but what really got her attention was the number of lemons loaded inside the machine’s rotating rack. The steady movement of the transparent rack, combined with the bright lighting and white body of the machine, gave off the appearance of some sort of futuristic lab.

At 500 yen (US$3.35) per cup, the juice is relatively pricey, but Haruka didn’t want to pass up this opportunity to try freshly squeezed lemon juice from a vending machine. So she made her electronic payment (the machine only accepts payments by credit card or QR code), and then an unexpected lemon performance began.

After pressing the purchase button, the machine moved on to the juice customisation screen, where there were three options to choose from, listed top to bottom as follows:

▼ Flavour – “Lemon” or “Salt Lemonade” / Sweetness – “Normal”, “Less”, “None” / Ice – “Normal”, “Less”, “None”

Since this was her first order, Haruka decided to opt for the standard “Lemon” flavour with “less sweetness” and “less ice”. After payment was completed, the rack began to rotate and one lemon was chosen in dramatic fashion.

▼ The fruit was placed on a glowing platform and slowly raised upwards, bathing the machine in a mysterious bluish-white glow.

▼ The lemon then dropped into a round opening with a little plop as it was sent off for squeezing.

It didn’t take long for a paper cup with a sealed plastic lid to appear in the collection slot, complete with a straw that was perfectly tucked into a U-shaped divot on the lid.

Though Haruka thought the straw might be too small for the cup, once she’d fully extended the bendable section…

▼ …it reached perfectly to the bottom of the drink. The package design was very clever and well thought-out.

After admiring all the unique details, Haruka now found herself having to try the beverage, and as someone who isn’t particularly good with sour flavours, she was a little nervous about taking her first sip.

▼ Surely the juice of an entire lemon would be far too sour to drink?

▼ After taking a deep breath and bracing herself for tartness, Haruka took a sip.

▼ To her surprise, it was actually delicious!

If she had to sum up the flavour in one sentence, she’d describe it as “a sweet-and-sour fresh juice that feels like it’s giving you a burst of energy”. The lemon flavour was certainly there, but it didn’t have the same sharp, piercing sourness as a freshly squeezed lemon – if anything, it was surprisingly smooth, with a “juice-like” quality that she thinks might even appeal to small children.

It was only the slight bitterness and oily residue from the lemon peel that indicated this was a freshly squeezed juice, and after taking a few more sips of it, the lingering aroma was so refreshingly pleasant that she began to wonder why lemon juice hasn’t caught on to become a more popular drink in Japan.

▼ Emboldened by her newfound taste for lemon juice, she decided to face her fears and order one with no sugar.

After watching the lemon show play out inside the machine again, Haruka reached for the new drink as soon as it was ready, and took a sip.

Hmm. It definitely wasn’t bad, but it also wasn’t delicious enough to make her want to purchase it again. For her, it seemed slightly underwhelming.

Though she’s not entirely sure, Haruka seems to think that the juices are diluted with water, so without sugar the flavour also becomes diluted, making it less satisfying as a juice. While health-conscious customers or those who want to enjoy the natural flavour of the fruit might prefer to order the drink without extra sweetness, Haruka says that she would recommend adding sugar. The sweetness seems to bring out the tartness of the lemon, making the citrus flavour seem more pronounced, and delicious as well.

At the end of the day, though, Haruka thoroughly enjoyed both drinks, and highly recommends trying them if you can. Right now, there are only a small number of “Peel-and-all Lemon Effect” machines installed across Japan, making them a rare vending machine find, so if you spot one, consider yourself lucky.

With its refreshing sweet-and-sour flavour, this is a great drink to enjoy on a hot day or as a refreshing palate cleanser after eating an oily meal like yakiniku (grilled meat). Plus, you could always try it out with a splash of something strong to create your own freshly made lemon sour, an iconic beverage in the Japanese drinks scene.

title: 7-Eleven Japan adds new chocolate fruit gummies to its sweets range, but are they worth the hype?
description: Convenience store chain has become the place to go for gummies, and fans are going wild for them. In recent years, 7-Eleven has carved out a niche for itself in the Japanese convenience store world as the place to go for gummies, specifically the exclusive chocolate-covered fruit gummy range known as “Chocotto Gummy“. A play […]
content:
Convenience store chain has become the place to go for gummies, and fans are going wild for them.

In recent years, 7-Eleven has carved out a niche for itself in the Japanese convenience store world as the place to go for gummies, specifically the exclusive chocolate-covered fruit gummy range known as “Chocotto Gummy“. A play on the words “choco to gummy” (“chocolate and gummy“) and “chokotto gummy” (“just a little gummy“), this range has become so popular that people have been known to buy multiple bags at a time.

▼ That popularity is set to continue with two brand new varieties: Okinawan Brown Sugar & Pineapple and Okinawan Brown Sugar & Mango.

Okinawa is famous for producing high-quality brown sugar in its tropical climate, but we weren’t sure how it would pair with chocolate gummies, so we decided to try both varieties to see how they would taste. The two packets, with their summery hibiscus motifs, look surprisingly similar at first glance so be careful not to grab the wrong one when you’re shopping.

▼ Let’s start the taste test with the Okinawan Brown Sugar & Pineapple.

▼ Each packet contains around 10 gummies.

With their beautiful, glossy chocolate coating, these look like solid chocolate balls, but when you lift one to your mouth, you get a slight scent of pineapple, which piques your curiosity as you take a bite.

The first thing you’ll taste is the sweetness of the chocolate, before the sweetly tart pineapple gummy component takes centre stage as you chew, making it feel like you’re eating a chunk of chocolate-covered pineapple. The Okinawan brown sugar is subtle, adding only a slight hint of flavour in the aftertaste. This is welcome news for gummy fans, as those with an aversion to the taste of brown sugar will hardly notice its presence, due to the well-balanced harmony between flavours.

▼ Next up is the Okinawan Brown Sugar & Mango.

▼Again, 10 chocolate-covered gummies inside.

From the second you open the bag, you’ll be engulfed in sweet, summery mango aromas, instantly lifting your mood with their deliciously fruity appeal. The gummy centre in each one is packed with the rich tropical flavour of mango, but when combined with the chocolate coating, the flavour becomes even deeper the longer you chew. As with the pineapple version, the brown sugar isn’t particularly noticeable, creating a nuanced flavour that appeals to adult tastes while making them incredibly easy to eat.

In fact, the ratio between fruit and chocolate is so perfect that it’s dangerously easy to keep munching on these. Whether you prefer the tartness of pineapple or the rich sweetness of mango, these gummies will satisfy your sweet cravings all summer long.

The combination of gummy and chocolate is like the best of both worlds, and they’re ready to perk you up at your nearest 7-Eleven, where they’re priced at 170 yen (US$1.15) each.

title: We tried Starbucks Japan’s new coffee for people who don’t drink coffee
description: Does the new “Clear Coffee” have what it takes to bring a non-coffee drinker into the fold? For many coffee drinkers, a cup of joe is a daily ritual – skip that morning cup and something just feels off. At the same time, though, more and more young people in Japan are said to be […]
content:
Does the new “Clear Coffee” have what it takes to bring a non-coffee drinker into the fold?

For many coffee drinkers, a cup of joe is a daily ritual – skip that morning cup and something just feels off. At the same time, though, more and more young people in Japan are said to be steering clear of coffee altogether, according to research conducted by Starbucks and Shibuya109 lab, a youth marketing organisation based in Tokyo’s Shibuya district.

▼ Participants enjoying some tasty market research.

In order to help bring those non-coffee drinkers into the fold, Starbucks has done something quite extraordinary: created a new line of coffee drinks for those who don’t like coffee.

Called Clear Coffee, there are two varieties to choose from – Standard and Citrus – both of which aim to appeal to anyone who’s ever been interested in coffee but always found it too bitter or intimidating to try. Made using Sumatra Masa Depan beans, a special blend created to mark Starbucks’ 30th anniversary in Japan this year, the coffee is extracted as a ristretto shot instead of an espresso shot, which concentrates the coffee’s sweetness and richness while reducing bitterness.

Our Japanese-language reporter K. Masami, who drinks at least one coffee a day, admits to usually gravitating towards rich, strong drinks. During the sweltering heat of summer, though, she tends to prefer lighter, more refreshing beverages, so she decided to try the new Clear Coffee to see if it really might be palatable for non-coffee drinkers.

Ordering the standard Clear Coffee, it looked much closer to an iced Americano than the chain’s regular iced brewed coffee, which makes sense because it’s prepared in a similar way by diluting coffee with water. In addition to containing a ristretto shot, it also contains Classic Syrup for sweetness, seeing as bitterness was said to be the main driving factor turning potential coffee converts away from traditional coffee.

Taking a sip, Masami found it had a gentle sweetness and an extremely clean finish. The bitterness had been noticeably toned down, but remarkably, the aroma of coffee was still present, creating a drink that felt unmistakably like coffee without overwhelming the palate. It was refreshing, didn’t leave a lingering aftertaste, and though it was lighter than a typical coffee, it still had enough body to avoid tasting watery.

The closest comparison Masami could think of was that it’s the coffee equivalent of Starbucks’ popular Chillax drinks, which are mellow, easy to drink and pleasantly refreshing.

After tasting the standard version, Masami could easily imagine the citrus working well with the drink’s light, refreshing character. However, seeing as the Clear Coffee already contains a shot of ristretto, she decided to avoid over-caffeinating herself and try the Citrus version another day.

So would she recommend the Clear Coffee? Well, if you’re someone who loves the bold bitterness of a traditional coffee, Clear Coffee may not completely satisfy your cravings. The coffee aroma is still there, though, so it doesn’t feel like you’re drinking a fake, flavoured beverage, and its lighter, sweeter profile makes it considerably easier to drink than a standard iced coffee. In that sense, if you’re a coffee lover who wants some lighter coffee refreshment, perhaps after you’ve already had your regular cup of joe, it’s a drink that’ll still interest your taste buds, especially if you know what to expect before diving in.

As for non-coffee drinkers, though, the Clear Coffee has a real chance of achieving what it sets out to do, acting as a gateway drink for those who wouldn’t otherwise think to order a coffee. It’s noticeably different from Starbucks’ usual coffee line-up, so it really does bridge the gap between bitter coffees and sweet lattes and Frappuccinos, which is something the chain wanted to address with the new release.

On sale from 31 July, the Clear Coffee is on the menu at 490 yen (US$3.30) for dine-in, while the Citrus Clear Coffee is slightly higher, at 590 yen. Both drinks are only available for a limited time.

title: Japanese popsicle experiment says eating one before going outside in summer helps keep you cool
description: Maker of Garigari-kun explores whether one of Japan’s favorite frozen treats can work as a pre-cooling agent. There’s an old adage that says the best time to fix your roof is when the sun is shining, a way of expressing that there are some things in life that are best dealt with before the potential […]
content:
Maker of Garigari-kun explores whether one of Japan’s favorite frozen treats can work as a pre-cooling agent.

There’s an old adage that says the best time to fix your roof is when the sun is shining, a way of expressing that there are some things in life that are best dealt with before the potential problem actually occurs. Of course, it can be hard to talk yourself into doing much of anything when that sun is shining on you with merciless summer fire, which brings us to a new piece of wisdom, which is that the best time to cool off with a popsicle is before you start to feel hot.

That’s the conclusion suggested by the results of an experiment conducted by Akagi Nyugyo. As fine dining connoisseurs are no doubt already aware, Akagi Nyugyo is a Japanese confectioner based in Saitama Prefecture and the maker of Garigari-kun (pictured above), one of Japan’s favorite brands of popsicle for the past several decades.

Even among frozen treats, Garigari-kun has a reputation as being especially refreshing in hot weather, with fans young and old ducking into convenience stores to buy one when out and about on scorching summer days. Recently, though, Akagi Nyugyo wondered ifs its flagship product could be applied to pre-cooling, cooling the body down before entering a high-temperature environment in order to lessen heat-related discomfort and fatigue. Working with professor Kazunobu Okazaki from Osaka Metropolitan University’s Urban Health and Sports Research Center, Akagi Nyugyo set up an experiment in which 61 men and women, ranging in ages from 20 to 59, first ate a Garigari-kun.

▼ If, after finding out that you could have been eating popsicles for the sake of science, you now find yourself asking “Have I been living my life wrong?”, don’t worry, we feel the same way.

After finishing their Garigari-kun, the study participants entered an enclosed room heated to summertime temperatures and performed light exercise.

When their session was finished, the participants were asked how they had felt during while exercising, and 59 percent said that they had felt cooler than they ordinarily do during similar levels of physical activity without having eaten a popsicle just prior to it. And with walking being a form of light exercise, Akagi Nyugyo is taking this as evidence that pre-cooling with a Garigari-kun before leaving your home or hotel in the summer can help your body better cope with the heat waiting for you in the outside environment.

The results make sense to Okazaki, who says that frozen confectionaries can be even more effective than chilled liquids at cooling the body from the inside, since an extra amount of heat gets absorbed in the melting process. In addition, while theoretically any frozen treat should be able to provide that benefit, the effect is especially strong with Garigari-kun because of how it’s made.

Look closely at the corner that’s been bitten off in the photo above, and instead of being a uniform solid, Garigari-kun is actually a popsicle-style outer layer with shaved ice inside. The fineness of the ice particles let them more easily travel down to the digestive tract, Okazaki says, where they can impart the largest cooling effects.

With all this in mind, Akagi Nyugyo is now pitching Garigari-kun not just as a way to cool off after coming home from a day out in the sun, but also as something to eat just before you head out for the day or step out of the office for on-site meetings with clients.

The experiment was actually conducted back in April, but Akagi Nyugyo apparently chose to wait on releasing the results until the summer heat hit, giving us new leverage in our demands to our boss that he keep a supply of professional-use popsicles in the office freezer.

Source: Akagi Nyugyo via Sankei Shimbun via Hachima Kiko

title: 7-Eleven Japan rethinks convenience store sandwiches with a wild new choc-mint variety
description: Convenience store chain tests our limits by turning the divisive flavour into a cream sandwich. In recent years, choc mint has become synonymous with summer in Japan, as the menthol component is believed to provide a cooling effect to help you feel refreshed during the hottest days of the year. It’s become such a common […]
content:
Convenience store chain tests our limits by turning the divisive flavour into a cream sandwich.

In recent years, choc mint has become synonymous with summer in Japan, as the menthol component is believed to provide a cooling effect to help you feel refreshed during the hottest days of the year. It’s become such a common flavour combination that there’s even a proud term for people who love it – “Chocominto”, a pun that sounds like the Japanese pronunciation of “Choc Mint” but uses the kanji “党” (“to”) for “political party”, to mean the “Chocolate Mint Party”.

Like many places in the world, though, choc mint remains a polarising flavour, as those who dislike it are quick to voice their opinions on it. However, if you are a member of the party, then 7-Eleven is here to support your choices with a new offering that might just test the limits of your loyalty: The Chocolate Mint Whipped Cream Sandwich.

Released as the latest flavour in the chain’s recently introduced “Yokubari Sandwich” (Greedy Sandwich”) line, which features generously filled single-serve sandwiches, this new choc-mint version uses hakka oil from Kitami Hakka Tsusho, a famous Hokkaido mint company.

Image: Kitami Hakka

Hakka oil is made from Japanese peppermint (“washu hakka”), and is known for its strong, clean mint aroma and powerful cooling sensation, due to its high menthol content.

The mint-green sticker on the sandwich will immediately spark the attention of locals who are familiar with the widely well-known brand, as it’s known to deliver a very intense mint hit. Though hakka oil has been used in some limited-edition drink collaborations before, this is our first time seeing it in the cream filling of a sandwich, making it a very rare treat in the Japanese sweets world.

Using a specially made chocolate bread, each bite is said to combine the sweetness of chocolate with the refreshing sensation of mint, while crushed chocolate chips mixed into the whipped cream add a contrast in texture.

Priced at 198 yen (US$1.30) plus tax, the new sandwich is sure to spark lively debate between not just those on either side of the choc-mint divide, but all lovers of Japanese sandwiches. After giving us chocolate sprinkle sandwiches with sakura pink bread, 7-Eleven is continuing to test traditional notions of what a sandwich can and should be, and we can’t wait to try it when it’s released at stores around Japan (unfortunately excluding Hokkaido and Okinawa) on 7 August.

title: Japan’s Super Volunteer, 86-year-old Haruo Obata, heads to the Kumamoto earthquake site
description: Your friendly neighborhood Super Volunteer. On 28 July, a 7.1 magnitude earthquake struck Kumamoto Prefecture, just outside of Kumamoto City. Having taken years to recover from a set of comparable earthquakes in 2016, being hit with another major one so soon completely undid a lot of that work. In addition, sweltering temperatures are making search […]
content:
Your friendly neighborhood Super Volunteer.

On 28 July, a 7.1 magnitude earthquake struck Kumamoto Prefecture, just outside of Kumamoto City. Having taken years to recover from a set of comparable earthquakes in 2016, being hit with another major one so soon completely undid a lot of that work. In addition, sweltering temperatures are making search and rescue efforts even more difficult and hazardous.

Against that backdrop, one man has decided to once again answer the call and drove out to the affected area to help. His name is Haruo Obata, and he’s been doing volunteer work in a number of capacities and all over the country for decades.

After retiring from his job as a fish merchant, he’s traveled around the country meeting people and helping out wherever he could, cleaning up nature trails, finding people’s lost belonging after disasters, and more. He shot to fame in 2018, after finding a missing two-year-old in Yamaguchi Prefecture in only about 30 minutes, and was dubbed Super Volunteer for his efforts ever since.

▼ Shortly after rescuing the child, Obata walked from Tokyo to his home in Oita, over 1,100 kilometers (680 miles) at the age of 79.

Since then, he seems to often pop up wherever a major disaster strikes and he’s within his ability to make it there. He’s been seen in the aftermath of the 2011 Tohoku Earthquake and even of Kumamoto Prefecture’s 2016 earthquakes. Now, living in nearby Oita Prefecture, the 86-year-old Obata is able to go to Kumamoto once again.

For those who aren’t familiar with Super Volunteer, this might seem concerning or even selfish on his part to inject himself into life-or-death situations, but Obata operates on a strict set of rules. In order to minimize his impact on disaster relief efforts, he tends to stay on the periphery and asks people who might otherwise get overlooked if he can do anything for them.

He also refuses to accept anything from residents. He brings his own food and supplies, sleeps in his car, and would never accept a dime from the people he helps, because what kind of Super Volunteer would do that?

However, by going to the disaster area, Obata is technically disobeying an order by the Kumamoto Prefectural government that volunteers stay away for the time being. This is not uncommon in such cases, as a sudden influx of people and supplies, especially non-essential ones, can cause disorder and do more harm than good.

Many readers of the news expressed in online comments that he is possibly buying too much into his own notoriety rather than looking out for others’ best interests. Others commented that even if he is acting perfectly selflessly, at his age it’s just not a good idea to get involved.

“I don’t care how super he is. If the governor says not to go, then don’t go. The heat is unbearable, there could be aftershocks, and there might even be a typhoon on the way.”
“Kumamoto summers are really hard, especially on someone his age. I hope he stays home.”
“I think his intentions are wonderful, but it might be time for him to retire.”
“If the prefecture is saying not to go, then he should act like a Super Volunteer and exercise the proper caution.”
“I get wanting to help, but at his age, if an aftershock happens, he’ll just be a burden.”
“I really appreciate what he’s doing, but they’re telling him not to go.”
“He’s not exactly an amateur at this. He’ll be fine.”
“Let him go. I hate how inflexible people in Japan can be. He already saved a life.”
“I can’t believe people on social media are bashing this guy who’s kept going for so long. You all just love tearing people down.”
“I respect his ability, but at his age it’s probably time to stop.”

Unfortunately, it seems like there is a big misconception about what Obata actually does in these situations, though. He’s not exactly running into ground zero of the worst hit areas, pushing firefighters aside, and trying to lift slabs of concrete by himself to get a piece of the spotlight.

▼ In this report from 2023, Obata helps a rural area that suffered widespread landslide damage in Fukuoka Prefecture and had a shortage of volunteers to help with the cleanup and repairs.

He got himself checked out at the hospital immediately before departing to Kumamoto to make sure he was fit to do so, and in the past, other rescue workers and residents of affected areas have praised Obata for his ability to do good without bothering others. He simply asks around to see if people need anything, even if it’s something as simple as helping clean up around a person’s home or helping find lost mementos.

That’s certainly enough for a person his age to handle, and in fact I’d say it’s a downright super thing to do.

title: Japan’s favorite popsicles add multilingual packaging to better connect with foreign tourists
description: Garigari-kun wants to make friends with/be eaten by people from all over the world. Garigari-kun is Japan’s favorite popsicle brand, and like a lot of sweets in Japan, part of that popularity comes from a revolving lineup of seasonal and limited-time flavors. One of the most popular versions of all just made its way back […]
content:
Garigari-kun wants to make friends with/be eaten by people from all over the world.

Garigari-kun is Japan’s favorite popsicle brand, and like a lot of sweets in Japan, part of that popularity comes from a revolving lineup of seasonal and limited-time flavors. One of the most popular versions of all just made its way back to convenience stores and supermarkets, and while the flavor is familiar to fans, the packaging is looking different, because it now features multiple foreign languages.

Garigari-kun Pear made its return on July 28, bringing with it the sweet and refreshing taste of Asian pear. Like all Garigari-kun offerings, it’s a squared-off popsicle shell on a stick that’s filled with shaved ice, but in the case of the pear flavor, there’s an even larger ratio of finely shaved ice to shell, to better evoke the sensation of biting into a crisp pear.

Garigari-kun has used the same uniquely enthusiastic-looking mascot character for decades, making him, and the product, instantly identifiable to Japanese shoppers. Foreign tourists in Japan, though, might not know who this kid with the jumbo-sized choppers is, so Garigari-kun maker Akagi Nyugyo has added text in a half-dozen foreign languages: English, simplified and traditional Chinese, Korean, Thai, and Spanish.

Oddly, the messages differ by language. The English exclamation, “A Japanese classic!”, focuses on Garigari-kun’s culinary cultural icon status without getting into details about its exact identity, while the Spanish one takes the opposite tack by letting you know that this is “Incredible shaved ice!”, and the Chinese proclamations want you to know how refreshing Garigari-kun is.

Still, any extra info is helpful for travelers who can’t read Japanese, and with the product name and flavor written in English/Latin alphabet text too, Akagi Nyugyo is hoping the new multilingual packaging will help catch travelers’ eyes and convince them to give Garigari-kun a try while they’re in Japan. Considering that there was a time not too long ago when fellow Japanese sweet snacks Pocky and Hi-Chew were virtually unknown to people outside their home country, it’s understandable that Akagi Nyugyo sees Japan’s ongoing inbound tourism boom as a chance for Garigari-kun to audition for a spot in the hearts of foodies from around the globe, especially with an increasing portion of foreign visitors traveling independently, as opposed to in group tours, and thus doing more of their own shopping in regular Japanese stores.

From August, Garigari-kun will also have multilingual ads in Narita Airport showing off their standard sky-blue “soda” (apple citrus) flavor. This one has a bit more information about the item itself, showing it in illustrated form and introducing it as “Japan’s famous ice candy” (though, as an American, I’d never heard the term “ice candy” before moving to Japan).

With Garigari-kun also being one of Japan’s most affordable frozen treats, the big hurdle in getting foreign tourists to try it really is getting them to know what it is. But for those who might still be on the fence, as part of its plans to better connect with visitors from overseas, Akagi Nyugyo will be giving out 6,000 free Garigari-kun, in soda and pear flavors, at Sensoji Temple in downtown Tokyo’s Asakusa neighborhood, one of the city’s biggest draws for international travelers, on August 5, starting at 9 a.m. And hey, the more people that know about Garigari-kun, the more people who can benefit from its recently observed pre-cooling properties.

title: Sweet dreams are made of cheese at this all-you-can-eat cheese and doria restaurant
description: Our stomachs are more than pleased after eating all of the cheese. Cheese can be a somewhat difficult product to find in Japan. Supermarkets generally stock only a few standard varieties, and anything imported comes with a hefty price tag. That’s why any deal that comes with unlimited cheese is likely to pique our interest […]
content:
Our stomachs are more than pleased after eating all of the cheese.

Cheese can be a somewhat difficult product to find in Japan. Supermarkets generally stock only a few standard varieties, and anything imported comes with a hefty price tag. That’s why any deal that comes with unlimited cheese is likely to pique our interest in a big way.

Our latest find is a series of eateries operated by the same parent company as the Saint Marc Cafe chain of ChocoCro fame. As of July 21, it has four restaurants that offer an all-you-can-eat cheese buffet for 70 minutes in Osaka, Okayama, Tokyo, and Fukuoka prefectures. One of those four and the one closest to our editorial office is Cheese & Doria Sweets in Tokyo’s upscale Jiyugaoka district. This branch is located within the De Aone shopping mall on the third floor.

Naturally, the only way we could satisfy our curiosity was to pay it a visit.

We took a seat inside and immediately grabbed a menu. While the all-you-can-eat cheese deal can be paired with a main dish like doria for an additional 550 yen…

…it can also be ordered on its own in two versions: the volume salad set (1,199 yen) or the all-you-can-drink wine set (1,639 yen). The former comes with your choice of one of three salads (grilled chicken colorful salad, bacon and Džiugas cheese caesar salad, ham and mozzarella cheese salad) and the latter with your choice of red or white wines. We opted for the volume salad set.

The biggest moment of anticipation was when we finally made our way over to the cheese corner, where eight different cheeses were laid out in a glorious spread. We decorated a plate with small samplings of each as artfully as we could.

The finished plate really highlighted how different all of them were. Pictured below, clockwise from the right, are: cottage cheese, dried fruits cream cheese, walnut mascarpone, basil cream cheese, and cheddar cheese (in the center). 

Continuing clockwise from the right are ricotta cheese, smoked cheese, and caramel mascarpone.

Viewed altogether, it was a truly cheesetastic plate.

Our first bite also told us that we didn’t have to worry about the taste–it lived up to the visuals.

Thankfully, the spread also came with unlimited crackers and baguette slices so we could balance the dairy with some carbs.

We were impressed because the bread was also high quality and made a wonderful accompaniment for the cheese.

By the way, there was a self-serve water station which offered a delightfully refreshing orange-flavored water as well.

After about ten minutes of slowly but steadily munching on the samples, the grilled chicken colorful salad we had ordered arrived. It was a decent size, bigger than a side salad for sure, and lived up to its colorful name.

The salad was delicious on its own, but we recommend adding some of the cheese to it as well. After testing several combinations, we found that the cottage cheese, basil cream cheese, and smoked cheese paired the best with it.

It was a very satisfying amount of ruffage with flavorful toppings that didn’t make us feel guilty about polishing off the whole bowl in no time at all.

OK, now back to the cheese. We wanted to try experimenting with some additional toppings, so we also grabbed some of the blueberry sauce, honey, and olive oil that were for the taking.

Drizzling them on certain cheeses served to amplify their deliciousness.

Among the combos, the dried fruits cream cheese paired with honey was a standout. We couldn’t help piling it on cracker after cracker.

Time was flying by. We wanted to make sure to get to the dessert cheeses before leaving so we pulled ourselves away from the honey cream cheese combo and turned to the sweetest offerings.

First up was the caramel mascarpone. The caramel lent a surprisingly bitter taste to the mix which resulted in a unique, sophisticated flavor.

This is a good time to share that the dessert cheese actually changes daily from one of six different offerings: granola cheese, blueberry yogurt cheese, satsumaimo (Japanese sweet potato) cream cheese, strawberry mascarpone, tiramisu-style cheese cream, and of course, the caramel mascarpone. They were all intriguing enough that it made us want to return in the future to sample them all.

Actually, at the register, we received an unexpected bonus in the form of some coupons for future visits. We guess a return visit really is in order!

All in all, binging on cheese was a fantastic way to spend a little over an hour on this day.

For another restaurant with an all-you-can-eat cheese deal, see this writeup of our recent visit to Tokyo’s Good Spoon Handmade Cheese & Pizzeria.

title: Pokémon comes to McDonald’s Japan for new Happy Meals toys, brings every generation’s starters
description: You can’t celebrate 30 years of Pokémon without 30 years of starters, plus a few more Pocket Monster all-stars. The Pokémon franchise is celebrating its 30th anniversary this year, and the latest partner in the birthday party is McDonald’s Japan, who’s just announced that brand-new Pokémon Happy Meals featuring 30 different Pokémon species are on […]
content:
You can’t celebrate 30 years of Pokémon without 30 years of starters, plus a few more Pocket Monster all-stars.

The Pokémon franchise is celebrating its 30th anniversary this year, and the latest partner in the birthday party is McDonald’s Japan, who’s just announced that brand-new Pokémon Happy Meals featuring 30 different Pokémon species are on the way.

In what’s become its standard style for big-name collaborations, McDonald’s will be releasing the Pokémon Happy Meals in three rounds. Six different toys will be available in the first, six more in the second, and then any of the 12 could be included in Happy Meals in round three. The toys will represent all 27 starter Pokémon that have appeared across the games’ nine generations so far, face-of-the-franchise Pikachu, Eevee, and Snorlax (who’s also getting time in the spotlight these days at the Pokémon Sleep event going on in Yokohama).

Round one kicks off with disc-shooting, ring toss, spinner, and rolling toys for the Kanto (Bulbasaur, Charmander, Squirtle), Johto (Chikorita, Cyndaquil, Totodile), Hoenn (Treecko, Torchic, Mudkip), Sinnoh (Turtwig, Chimchar, Piplup), and Unova (Snivy, Tepig, Oshawott) starters. The Pikachu Poké Ball Roller is part of this group too, with Pikachu adorably wagging his tail back and forth as you push the ball forward.

Round two brings with it more spinners and shooters for the Kalos (Chespin, Fennekin, Froakie), Alola (Rowlet, Litten, Popplio), Galar (Grookey, Scorbunny, Sobble), and Paldea (Sprigatito, Fuecoco, Quaxly) region starters, as well as the Eevee Poké Ball Roller…

…and Snorlax Name Tag, which you can clip to your or anyplace else where you want to simultaneously deliver the messages “This belongs to me” and “I love the sleepiest Pokémon.”

▼ There’s space underneath なまえ (“name”) for you to write your name.

The Pokémon 30th anniversary Happy Meals come after last month’s McDonald’s Japan Summer Chance Bag, which included items such as a Pikachu French fry timer and color-changing Pokémon beverage cups.

Round one starts on August 7 and round two on August 14. Round three begins on August 21 and runs for an indefinite amount of time, ostensibly until stock of the toys runs out, which likely won’t be very long. If you’re looking to get some for yourself, keep in mind that in order to deter scalpers, McDonald’s Japan will be limiting purchases to six Happy Meals per customer group on August 7, 8, and 9, and online orders will be limited to the official McDonald’s Delivery Service on those days as well. Though not yet announced, similar policies will likely also be in effect when round two starts.

title: Is covering your entire upper body with cooling strips enough to fend off Japan’s summer heat?
description: Mr. Sato thinks it might be, and when was the last time he had an idea that didn’t pan out? “All right everybody, patch me up!” As loyal readers know, some very strange things can happen at SoraNews24 headquarters. Even by our standards, though, it was pretty startling to see our ace reporter Mr. Sato […]
content:
Mr. Sato thinks it might be, and when was the last time he had an idea that didn’t pan out?

“All right everybody, patch me up!”

As loyal readers know, some very strange things can happen at SoraNews24 headquarters. Even by our standards, though, it was pretty startling to see our ace reporter Mr. Sato whip off his shirt and issue this command to everyone in earshot. Of course, he had a perfectly logical reason for his behavior, or at least a perfectly Sato-like reason for it, so let’s go back a few steps and follow his thought process.

For a while there, it felt like we were in for a mild summer in Japan this year. The June “rainy season” had been cooler and dryer than usual, and even once we’d gotten into July the temperature and humidity were still pretty tolerable. But since about a week and a half ago, it’s like the weather has been making up for lost time, with a massive heat wave mercilessly baking much of the country with consecutive days with daytime highs over 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit).

This had all of us looking for relief from the heat, and Mr. Sato’s first instinct was to go out on the office balcony and try to intimidate the sun itself into going easier on us.

▼ “Hey, sun! Give it a rest already, will ya? You want me to have to smack you around a little, huh?”

Unfortunately, due to Mr. Sato lacking the necessary arm length to make good on his threat and/or the sun lacking ears with which to hear it, the hot weather continued. So it was back to the drawing board, but thanks to his uniquely active brain, it wasn’t long until he hit on an even more promising plan than celestial violence.

Excited and energized by his own brilliance, Mr. Sato dashed out the door…

…and returned shortly bearing boxes…

…boxes of cooling strips.

Often called “Hiepita” (though that’s actually the name of one specific discontinued brand), these adhesive patches can be commonly found in Japanese drugstores and convenience stores. Originally marketed as a way to cope with fever symptoms, people also discovered that their cooling sensation can be a way to cope with weather-related heat as well. The orthodox way to use them is to place one, and only one, across your forehead, but with extreme weather calling for, in Mr. Sato’s judgement, extreme measures, he had a more ambitiously abundant strategy in mind, which brings us up to the point in this tale where he commanded…

“All right everybody, patch me up!”

Again, even on the Sato scale, this was a pretty weird one, and the initial response from the in-office staff this day was less than enthusiastic.

But Mr. Sato would not be denied. “C’mon, get your butts in gear and get to patching!” he ordered, and while his insistence didn’t necessarily produce what you’d call obedience, it did convince everyone being press-ganged into this project that it’d be easier to just slap some patches on the guy than it would be to talk him out of it.

▼ “OK, let’s get this over with.”

“So we can just put ‘em wherever, right?” asked fellow reporter Seiji Nakazawa, but Mr. Sato quickly shot down such flippancy, rhetorically asking “Don’t you know you’re supposed to put your heart into this?”

▼ No, Seiji did not know that.

With his back now covered in cooling strips, the team thought that they were done, but Mr. Sato continued to stand there waiting. “Uh, you want us to do your front too?” asked P.K. Sanjun, triggering a snappy “Obviously!” from Mr. Sato.

“What do you mean ‘obvious’? You could do your front yourself, you know,” protested P.K., which earned him an exasperated “You don’t get it, do you? I want everyone to do this for me.”

At this point, we started to become unsure how much of this was a genuine attempt to cool down and how much of it was just a power trip, but one thing was clear.

Mr. Sato was feeling very good.

▼ “Yes! It’s happening! My own personal winter!”

In total, we had placed 68 cooling patches on Mr. Sato’s body. After basking for a few moments in the icy sensations, Mr. Sato once again headed towards the door, commanding us to follow for the second round of testing.

He remained comfortably cool as we rode the elevator down to the first floor of the building (though, to be honest, riding the cramped, slow, and shaky elevator in our building is always kind of a chilling experience). After exiting the elevator, he strode confidently towards the door to the street to see if his cooling strip countermeasure could stand up to the powerful direct sunlight of a Tokyo summer afternoon.

Granted, this isn’t the strangest attire one of our reporters has worn in public, but it’s still in the top 10. “From behind, it kind of looks like you’re wearing some sort of armor” observed Ahiruneko, to which Mr. Sato replied “I know, right?”

▼ We’re not sure how he knew what he looked like from behind, so we’re adding “Does he have eyes in the back of his head?” to the to-be-investigated topics in the Mr. Sato mystery file.

Finally, we arrived at the park near SoraNews24 HQ. Like a lot of small urban parks in Japan, it’s mainly concrete, gravel, and play equipment, with no grassy lawn and most of its trees only providing a thin strip of shade on the outside edge of its area.

The central section is basically its own little heat island, so it was here that Mr. Sato threw out his arms and dared the sun to do its worst.

“Hey, sun, that all you got, huh?”

“You aint so hot!”

“I can’t even feel you anymore! Bwahahahahaha!”

At this point, there are probably a few things that our lawyers would probably like us to point out, starting with the fact that, officially, we do not recommend Mr. Sato’s idea, especially on a regular basis. For one thing, heat is only one of the potential hazards presented by intense sunlight. UV rays are also a concern, and even if all those cooling patches were making Mr. Sato feel cool, the exposed gridwork of skin between them was still getting roasted. Another thing to keep in mind is that cooling strips don’t always actually lower your body temperature to the same degree as the sudden sensation they provide would suggest, so sticking six dozen or so of them on yourself isn’t really a safe way of avoiding heat exhaustion, as it’s not a substitute for proper hydration and staying out of direct sunlight during the hottest parts of the day.

On the other hand, a single cooling strip, perhaps attached to your back or chest where it can be covered by clothing, can be quite refreshing. As for whether the absurd amount Mr. Sato used is a smart idea, well, he did feel very cool standing in the park…

…but he also ended up trying to have an extended conversation with the sun itself, so if you don’t want to fry your brain, there are better ways to cope with the summer heat.

title: Coco’s Japan is very confident in their chilled ramen, but should they be? [Taste test]
description: Premium-priced hiyashi chuka comes to the American coffee shop’s Japanese branches. With the summer heat hitting Japan in full force, it’s time to look for ways to stay cool however you can, even when you’re eating, and recently that search took us to Coco’s to try their chilled ramen. And just to be clear, when […]
content:
Premium-priced hiyashi chuka comes to the American coffee shop’s Japanese branches.

With the summer heat hitting Japan in full force, it’s time to look for ways to stay cool however you can, even when you’re eating, and recently that search took us to Coco’s to try their chilled ramen. And just to be clear, when we say “Coco’s,” we’re not talking about Japanese curry rice restaurant chain Coco Ichibanya. No, we’re actually talking about Coco’s, the American coffee shop that also has branches in Japan.

In its home country, Coco’s is known for reliably tasty, but not necessarily adventurous, American fare. Bacon-and-egg breakfasts, burgers with French fries, slices of apple pie, those kinds of things. But as is sometimes the case when restaurant chains from the U.S. cross the Pacific, Coco’s Japan has a more varied, and also upscale, menu, and right now that includes hiyashi chuka, a chilled ramen dish that Japan loves eating in the summer.

Not only is Coco’s Japan serving chilled ramen, they’re very confident in its quality, as they’re asking 1,419 yen (US$8.75) for it. It’s possible to find hiyashi chuka for close to half that price at casual restaurants, so in setting the price that high, Coco’s has set the bar pretty high for itself.

Coco’s does offer some special ingredients to justify its premium pricing, though. For starters, the standard hiyashi chuka toppings are egg, cucumber, tomato, and ham. Coco’s replaces that last one, though, with roast beef, a much fancier ingredient.

You also get some nice, big shrimp…

…wakame (seaweed)…

…and even okra, which is something we’d never encountered in hiyashi chuka before this.

The presentation is quite beautiful, and we rotated our bowl around to get a good, appreciative look at the chilled ramen from every angle. Having passed the visual test, it was time to move on to the taste test, performed by our Japanese-language writer Takashi Harada, and he’s happy to report that Coco’s hiyashi chuka tastes every bit as good as it looks!

There are quite a few different flavors involved in hiyashi chuka, with even the chilled, vinegary broth having both sweet and sour elements to it. Too much of any one aspect can make the entire meal feel off, but everything here works perfectly together. Takashi was especially impressed by the quality of the tomatoes and okra, which had no unpleasant acidity or bitterness, so much so that he’s now convinced that okra can be a viable addition to the dish. Likewise, roast beef turned out to be an ingenious addition, especially with the little dab of sweet sauce that Coco’s applies to the meat.

The noodles are excellent too, thin and with just the right amount of firmness. And if you want your chilled ramen to still bring some heat to your taste buds, you get a side dish with some very hot spicy mustard if you want to mix it in.

So Coco’s hiyashi chuka isn’t just better than one might expect, but, simply put, very good hiyashi chuka. If you’re looking for something to both fill you up and cool you off this summer, it’s very much worth its price…and if noodles aren’t your thing, they’ve got other traditionally Japanese ways to cool off too.

title: Sanrio characters join forces with your favorite Japanese snack mascots as prizes at Family Mart

content:
The convenience store chain offers the summer’s most kawaii collab by bringing 26 characters from different worlds together.

Major Japanese convenience store chain Family Mart is celebrating its 45th anniversary in September with some of the cutest, most recognizable mascots out there!

As of August 4, Family Mart locations across Japan are hosting a Sanrio characters and manufacturers’ mascots campaign. Buying eligible products will allow you to receive promotional prizes, and saving up stamps from showing your FamiPay app at the time of purchase will earn you entries in a lottery for more prizes. Plus, there will be limited-time Sanrio goods for anyone to purchase.

▼ The campaign designs pair 13 popular Sanrio characters with 13 mascots of famous snack brands. What a fun, one-of-a-kind souvenir those would be to bring home–especially for any hardcore snackers!

First, let’s focus on the promotional prizes you can receive with purchase of two eligible products. How do you know which products are eligible for the campaign? That’s easy–just look for this bright green label on applicable items in the store:

The prizes will arrive in two rounds and in two different forms–acrylic keychains and cloth drawstring pouches–as detailed below. They will be randomly distributed to customers making qualified purchases.

Round 1 began on August 4 at 10 a.m. and with eight acrylic keychains.

The Sanrio/snack pairings here are:
● Hello Kitty x Koala’s March (Lotte’s Koala March)
● Little Twin Stars x Noppo Toppochan (Lotte’s Toppo)
● Kuromi x Petagoo (Nobel Seika’s Petagoo Gumi)
● Hanamaruobake x Hachinosuke (Nobel Seika’s Hachimitsu Kinkan Nodoame)
● Cinnamoroll x Potta (Calbee’s Jagabee)
● Cogimyun x Kappaebikun (Calbee’s Kappaebisen)
● My Melody x Apollochan (Meiji’s Apollo)
● Badtz-Maru x Hiiobaachan (Koikeya’s Karamucho)

Round 2 begins on August 18 at 10 a.m. with five more acrylic keychains.


● Tuxedo Sam x Mr. P (Kellogg Japan’s Pringles)
● Ahiru no Pekkle x Kyorochan (Morinaga Seika’s Chocoballs)
● Usahana x Totomaru (Morinaga Seika’s Ottotto)
● Pochacco x Chikin Ramen Hiyokochan (Nissin Shokuhin’s Chikin Ramen)
● Hangyodon x Demaeboya (Nissin Shokuhin’s Demaeiccho)

Round 2 will also have cloth drawstring pouches. The pouches come in a pink version and a green version, with six of the collaborative designs on the former and seven on the latter.

Second, let’s take a look at the fabulous prizes you could win by saving up enough stamps to enter the prize lotteries. To gain stamps, simply display your FamiPay app while making an eligible purchase. Each purchase will grant you one stamp. You can enter three different lotteries depending on the number of stamps you’ve saved up which each result in a different prize. This part of the campaign runs from August 4 through August 31, and you can enter the lottery between August 4 and September 4.

● 5-stamp lottery
Prize: Storage box with 13 items / 20 winners
The “grand prize” is a reusable box that pays homage to the campaign’s designs. What’s inside is a special secret waiting for the winners…!

Winners can print their stickers on sticker paper using their gifted code between September 24 and October 15 at any of Family Mart’s multi-function printing machines.

● 2-stamp lottery
Prize: Family Mart points worth 500 yen (US$3.18) / 100 winners
It’s not much, but it’s yours to spend however you’d like.

Third, Family Mart will also offer special Sanrio goods for anyone to purchase for the duration of the campaign, including plenty of puffy stickers that have been all the rage in Japan recently. Please note that the availability of certain items may differ slightly within different stores.

990 yen / On sale August 4
These puffy nail accessories add a fun texture to anyone’s manicure. The two versions are Hello Kitty (red and black-bowed) or My Melody and Kuromi.

▼ Pictured below: Hello Kitty version

528 yen / On sale August 7
Each puffy sticker has five sparkly rhinestones attached to it for when you’re feeling extra fancy.

● Hello Kitty sparkly capsule stickers (4 kinds)
528 yen / On sale August 7
Filled with sequins and glitter powder on the inside and gold and silver foil stamping on the outside, these stickers certainly make a statement.

● Sanrio characters clear candy stickers (4 kinds)
528 yen / On sale August 7
These puffy stickers with silver foil stamping on a clear background are perfect for decorative touches or for showing off in your sticker collection case.

● Sanrio character encyclopedia stickers (2 kinds)
528 yen / On sale August 7
With the characters’ names written on the removeable backing sheets, these puffy sticker sheets can be folded to display as your very own character encyclopedia.

● Sanrio characters candy stickers (5 kinds)
550 yen / On sale August 7
Stickers of popular Sanrio characters eating sweets? Yes, please, with a cherry on top!

● Sanrio characters slide mirror keychain
990 yen / On sale August 20
Group A: one out of seven randomly selected, Group B: one out of six randomly selected
Mini mirrors that are designed to mimic stained glass cookies are equally stylish and practical.

We have to say–we think that Family Mart really hit the kawaii jackpot with this latest campaign. We can’t wait to get snacking and packing prizes of our favorite mascots!

content:
JAL and ANA among carriers to start requiring earlier baggage check-in very soon.

The convenience of using Haneda Airport isn’t just its close proximity to downtown Tokyo, it’s also how easy the station is to access by train. There’s a station right in the basement of the building, with elevators that will take you right from the platform up into the departure lobbies, and when you add in how punctual and reliable Japan’s rail networks are, it can be easy to assume you don’t need to build much buffer space into your schedule when you’re heading to Haneda to catch a flight.

However, several airlines that fly out of Haneda, including JAL and ANA, have put out a reminder that there’s a limit to how close you can cut things, as they’ve announced that they’ll be instituting stricter deadlines for checking in bags for domestic flights, and they’ll be going into effect very soon.

Under the new policy, JAL, ANA, Air Do, StarFlyer, Solaseed Air, and Japan Transocean Air will be moving back their baggage check-in deadline by an additional 10 minutes, with the new deadline being 30 minutes before the flight’s departure time. Note that this is not a suggested time, but a hard cutoff, implying that passengers with bags to check who show up at the counter with less than 30 minutes to spare before departure will be faced with a choice between missing their flight or leaving their bags behind.

In addition to the six airlines mentioned above, Skymark says that while it is currently sticking with its baggage check-in cutoff of 20 minutes before departure, it will be monitoring the situation and moving up the deadline if it becomes necessary to do so. All seven airlines have also issued statements reminding passengers that their flight’s scheduled departure time indicates the time at which the plane is slated pull away from the gate, and so passengers are expected to be boarded at least 10 minutes prior to departure.

At the moment, the policy change applies only to domestic routes, but with the change coming as part of a renewed effort to maintain punctual takeoff times, there’s a chance that JAL and ANA will be keeping an eye on whether or not similar changes are necessary to keep its international flights on time. So again, while it can be tempting to time you arrival at Haneda so that you roll up at the last possible moment before you need to be there, the wise thing to do is to actually arrive a little earlier, especially since there’s usually something cool to see at the airport.

title: Toyota Museum’s international retro vehicle parade returns to Aichi this autumn
description: Cruise over to Moricoro Park for 120 vintage cars or apply and show off your own pre-1997 classic. The Toyota Motor Corporation is a household name in much of the world for being the largest automobile manufacturer on a global scale, but has also had a big impact back at home. Rooted deep in Aichi […]
content:
Cruise over to Moricoro Park for 120 vintage cars or apply and show off your own pre-1997 classic.

The Toyota Motor Corporation is a household name in much of the world for being the largest automobile manufacturer on a global scale, but has also had a big impact back at home. Rooted deep in Aichi Prefecture, the city of Koromo renamed itself Toyota City in 1959 to honor the company, its primary engine of growth. Just down the road from the city, in neighboring Nagakute City, sits the Toyota Automobile Museum, an institution that seeks to preserve global car history across every manufacturer and era, well beyond Toyota’s own lineage. That’s not to be confused with the nearby Toyota Kaikan Museum that focuses on Toyota products and services, as well as the latest Toyota and Lexus models.

On November 15, the 36th Toyota Automobile Museum Classic Car Festival makes its return, promising an unforgettable experience celebrating automotive history at Expo 2005 Aichi Commemorative Park, also known as Morocoro Park, which also plays host to the fantastical Ghibli Park.

The festival starts with a 14-kilometer (8.7-mile) parade featuring between 100 to 120 preserved classic cars rolling through public streets, starting at 7:00 a.m. from the museum.

Once the parade arrives at Moricoro Park, you can take a closer look at the vintage Japanese and international gems. Owners of the cars will be mingling around looking to chat about their beloved rides, sometimes wearing period attire, or setting up some custom memory panels to explain more about the car’s history. With food trucks, local booths, and the lush park grounds, it all makes for a fantastic day out for friends and family.

While official spectator entrance details for 2026 are still pending, looking back at the 35th festival, which was held in spring 2025, admission to the exhibition was completely free, so if you’re a lover of classic cars, you’re likely to be in for some budget-friendly fun.

If you happen to own a classic car in Japan, it’s possible to get in on the action yourself. Any Japanese or imported cars produced in or before 1996 (excluding motorcycles) are eligible, but vehicles must be street-legal and in a driveable state on the day of the event. Propellers and flotation devices are not proof of roadworthiness, no matter how phantasmagorical a machine it may be.

Applications for participation open from August 5 to August 15 via the official Toyota Automobile Museum website. If selected for one of the limited spots available, the participation fee is 5,000 yen (US$31.38), which covers the official parade number, a commemorative badge, and event pamphlet.

Whether you want to take a trip down memory lane or are in the mood to experience some history, you won’t be needing 1.21 gigawatts to feel the nostalgia, just head on down to Moricoro Park this November.

title: Pokémon Center Online designates first Pokémon items that will require Japanese ID card to buy
description: Fans will need to be residents of Japan in order to buy these items from the Pokémon Center Online. Scalping is becoming an increasingly large problem for the Pokémon franchise, and the latest move by the Pokémon Company to clamp down on the practice is a new system that requires a Japanese government-issued ID card […]
content:
Fans will need to be residents of Japan in order to buy these items from the Pokémon Center Online.

Scalping is becoming an increasingly large problem for the Pokémon franchise, and the latest move by the Pokémon Company to clamp down on the practice is a new system that requires a Japanese government-issued ID card for making certain purchases through the Pokémon Center Online store. As unveiled last month, the system works in tandem with the Digital Identification App, an app created by the Digital Agency (part of the prime minster’s cabinet) and the My Number Card, a government-issued ID card that’s also used in the administration of social services such as health insurance and social security/national pension payments.

The Pokémon Center Online has now announced the first items which will require shoppers to prove their identity through the Digital App, with four Pokémon Card Game items designated for such protection, all of them part of the Pokémon Card Game’s 30th Celebration series and scheduled to go on sale next month. The restricted items are:

● Pokémon Card Game Mega Expansion Pack 30th Celebration Box (7,200 yen [US$46])
● Pokémon Card Game Mega 30th Celebration Futuristic Box (27,500 yen)
● Pokémon Card Game Mega 30th Celebration Espeon and Umbreon Premium Deck Set (6,200 yen)
● Pokémon Card Game Mega 30th Celebration Card Set (9-type complete set) (10,800 yen)

▼ The Futuristic Box is a bundle that includes two guaranteed Pikachu ex promo cards, card shields, a deck case, and a play mat, and a display case, among other items.

▼ The Pokémon Card Game Mega 30th Celebration Espeon and Umbreon Premium Deck Set features two ex cards of Espeon and Umbron each, part of two separate decks with a grand total of 60 cards.

Now, if you’re wondering how non-residents of Japan can get a My Number Card and use the Digital Identification App, the answer is that they can’t. So in requiring verification through the app, the Pokémon Center Online is effectively restricting sales of the affected items to Japanese residents only.

That’s an unhappy side effect, but odds are the Pokémon Company imagines that legitimate foreign fans aren’t likely to be getting shut out of making the purchases. While visiting tourists do indeed drop a lot of cash on Pokémon stuff in Japan, merch such as Pokémon plushies, T-shirts, and even Happy Meal toys are the big draws for fans from overseas. Pokémon cards sold in Japan explain the card’s capabilities in Japanese text only, so the language barrier makes them of limited appeal or utility for foreign fans who’re actually interested in using them to play the game, which would suggest that foreign shoppers who are buying and limited-edition cards/card sets are doing so for some other purpose. On the other hand, it could be that the Pokémon Center Online’s decision to require use of the Digital Identification App is simply because it’s Japan’s most extensive domestic platform for electronic identity verification, thus making it the most easily available infrastructure for tracking repeat/bulk purchases by the same person, regardless of nationality.

▼ The Pokémon Card Game Mega 30th Celebration Card Sets come in nine versions, with a guaranteed set of cards representing a single generation’s starter Pokémon, a display stand, and two packs of cards.

It’s not clear whether physical Pokémon Center stores in Japan will also require buyers to use the Digital Identification App/a My Number Card in order to make purchases. No other retailers currently have any such requirements in place, but may enact their own sort of anti-scalping methods.

Pre-orders for the restricted item open on August 10 for the Pokémon Card Game Mega Expansion Pack 30th Celebration Box, 30th Celebration Futuristic Box, and 30th Celebration Espeon and Umbreon Premium Deck Set with a slated shipping date of September 15, with the respective dates for the Pokémon Card Game Mega 30th Celebration Card Sets are August 28 and October 15.

title: Yoshinoya gets into fancy fish, but is the cheap beef king reaching too far? [Taste test]
description: Japan’s biggest beef bowl chain is now serving up simmered kinmedai. When people think of Yoshinoya, they think of beef, and not just any beef, but cheap beef. That’s not to say Yoshinoya’s beef bowls are low-quality or bad-tasting, but the chain’s flagship fare is definitely more “good honest grub” than “fine dining.” So we […]
content:
Japan’s biggest beef bowl chain is now serving up simmered kinmedai.

When people think of Yoshinoya, they think of beef, and not just any beef, but cheap beef. That’s not to say Yoshinoya’s beef bowls are low-quality or bad-tasting, but the chain’s flagship fare is definitely more “good honest grub” than “fine dining.”

So we were surprised, and intrigued, when we found out that Yoshinoya is now also serving up fancy fish.

On July 27, Yoshinoya added the Gyu Kinmedai no Nizuke Teishoku, or Beef and Simmered Sea Bream Set Meal, to its menu. Kinmedai specifically is the Japanese name for the fish called splendid alfonsino in English, but no matter which moniker you use, it’s a premium variety of seafood, prized for its natural sweetness and satisfyingly substantial texture.

Finding the kinmedai set meal took a bit of sifting through the menu. The touchscreen terminal used for ordering at the Yoshinoya branch we visited didn’t mention the new item on its top screen, nor did we find it in the “limited-time specials” section. Instead, it was mixed in with the other options in the teishoku (定食) set meals tab. 899 yen (US$5.50) gets you a simmered kinmedai fillet, white rice, a bowl of miso soup, and a plate of Yoshinoya’s classic simmered beef which ordinarily tops its beef bowls. Alternatively, there’s a 799-yen version of the kinmedai set that skips the beef and gives you a plate of pickles in its place, but we opted for the full 899-yen set.

Size-wise, we were happy with the kinmedai fillet. Given how kinmedai isn’t something that’s even available at budget-friendly fast food restaurants, Yoshinoya only giving you a tiny sliver of the stuff wouldn’t have been a shock, but this was a decently sized slice, and a visually bountiful one too.

Most importantly, though, it was also a delicious slice of kinmedai! Slow-cooked in a traditional soy sauce-based simmer sauce, the fish is imparted with sweet and salty notes, and while it might not quite match what you’d get at a fancy seafood specialty restaurant or a portside eatery where the fish just came off the boat an hour ago, Yoshinoya’s kinmedai still has an excellent flavor. Basically, anyone who likes kinmedai will like this, and the fact that it’s available at such an accessible chain as Yoshinoya is incredible.

Though the fish is served on its own plate, we highly recommend letting some of the sauce drip onto the rice, since it’s so good that you won’t want to let a single drop go to waste.

Something has to be seriously tasty to make the beef in a Yoshinoya set meal feel like a supporting part instead of the main attraction, but that’s definitely what happens here. While this isn’t the very first time for Yoshinoya to serve up fish (they include salmon in some of their breakfast sets, for example), it is their first time to offer such a fancy fish as kinmedai.

So yeah, this is definitely worth digging through the menu to find. Just be aware that even though the Beef and Simmered Sea Bream Set Meal is listed with the regular set meals, it is in fact a limited-time item, though one without an announced specific ending date, so you’ll want to try it while you can.

title: U.S. government reportedly planning to close Nagoya consulate
description: Move would leave Japan’s fourth-largest city without consular services. With a population of roughly 2.3 million people, Nagoya is the fourth-largest city in Japan. It also holds an extremely important position in Japanese industry and its connections to the global economy, by nature of being the closest major city to the head office of Toyota […]
content:
Move would leave Japan’s fourth-largest city without consular services.

With a population of roughly 2.3 million people, Nagoya is the fourth-largest city in Japan. It also holds an extremely important position in Japanese industry and its connections to the global economy, by nature of being the closest major city to the head office of Toyota and many of the automakers factories and suppliers.

Nevertheless, the U.S. government is planning to close its consulate in Nagoya, according to a report from Reuters citing sources who spoke under condition of anonymity.

According to the report, the U.S. State Department has sent notices to multiple congressional committees informing them of its intent to close the Nagoya consulate, as well as the U.S. embassy in Granada, consulates in Canada (Winnipeg) and Indonesia (Medan), and an embassy branch office in Cameroon (Douala). The downsizing does not appear to be tied to any diplomatic disagreements and to instead be a cost-cutting move by the U.S. government.

Shutting down the Nagoya consulate would leave the full embassy in Tokyo and and the consulate in Osaka as the nearest alternatives, both of which are roughly and hour and a half away from Nagoya by Shinkansen, and even lengthier trips by more affordable modes of transportation.

Closing the Nagoya consulate would not likely have an immediate or significant impact on the lives of most American citizens living in the area, however. Passport renewal, the most commonly required government service by Americans living abroad, is already handled by mail, with no in-person, on-site renewal option available. Overseas voting for U.S. elections is also a by-mail only affair. As of last year, U.S. consulates and embassies in Japan no longer offer notarization services for “affidavits of competency to marry,” a form requested by the Japanese government when foreigners are getting married in Japan, and instead provides an online form that can be downloaded online stating that the U.S. government has no such certification system.

All of which is to say that many American expats can live in Japan for years, or even decades, without ever having to physically go to a consulate or embassy. Even for those who do need to visit a U.S. government office in-person, the U.S. Embassy and Consulates in Japan website already informs them that “The U.S. Consulate in Nagoya no longer provides American Citizens Services,” and directs them to the Osaka consulate instead.

As such, the Nagoya consulate’s role is more diplomatic liaison than service provider, facilitating cultural exchange and establishing ties with local educational, scientific, and business organizations.

▼ Recent posts from the U.S. consulate in Nagoya have highlighted chief consul Anna Wang visiting a Mitsubishi Heavy Industries facility in the city…

ワン首席領事が、名古屋市の三菱重工業大江工場を訪問し、民間機セグメントの皆さまと意見交換しました。ボーイング787「ドリームライナー」の主翼構造材「ウィングボックス」は、長年にわたりすべてここで製造されています。日米の航空宇宙産業パートナーシップを支える重要な取り組みです。… pic.twitter.com/xR4gRFNdA2

— 在名古屋米国領事館首席領事 (@USConsNagoya) July 21, 2026

▼ …and a visit to Nagoya by an American youth baseball team as part an international sister cities program.

7月12日、四日市ドームにてロングビーチと四日市のリトルリーグチームによる交流親善試合が開催されました！ 領事館からはアメリカ建国記念キャップとボールを提供し、1963年から続く両市の姉妹都市交流を祝いました。 日米の友情がこれからも続いていきますように！ pic.twitter.com/WthiUc370P

— 在名古屋米国領事館首席領事 (@USConsNagoya) July 14, 2026

So no, closing the Nagoya consulate is unlikely to trigger an immediate crisis for American expats in terms of accessing government services, nor will it bring an immediate halt to international cultural exchange. That said, it’s not going to make those things easier either, and it’ll be a sad development if the consulate does end up being deemed an unacceptable expense.
